interest: This file offers historians exceptional insight into how U.S. diplomats and international scientific experts systematically dismantled the primary economic justification for Japanese imperial expansion in the interwar era. Both Dr. Egerton Charles Grey's League of Nations study in 1927 and Consul E. R. Dickover's penetrating 1932 analyses reveal that Japan was overwhelmingly self-sufficient in foodstuffs, with net per capita food imports vastly lower than those of Western European nations and the United States. Dickover's empirical demolition of the 'Manchurian life-line' thesis—demonstrating that net food imports from Manchuria amounted to a negligible four cents per person annually—provides historians with compelling contemporary documentation of how Malthusian anxiety and false claims of imminent starvation were manufactured and deployed to rationalize aggression in China.
overview: This file comprises diplomatic despatches, an expert League of Nations study, and detailed consular economic analyses from 1927 and 1932 evaluating Japan's food supply, agricultural capacity, and degree of dependence on foreign foodstuffs. In August 1927, U.S. Ambassador Charles MacVeagh forwarded a published study from The Japan Advertiser by Dr. Egerton Charles Grey, who investigated Japan's food resources on behalf of the League of Nations Health Section and concluded that Japan experienced no genuine food shortage, as net cereal imports were under five percent of consumption and could readily be offset by reducing rice polishing, curbing sake brewing, or reclaiming mulberry acreage. In 1932, American Consul E. R. Dickover in Kobe followed up with an extensive statistical report and an accompanying popular article titled 'The Wolf at Japan's Door,' explicitly refuting the Japanese government's claim that overpopulation and food scarcity necessitated military expansion into Manchuria. By comparing net per capita food imports across Western Europe, the United States, and Japan, Dickover proved that Japan was far more self-sufficient than European nations and that net food imports from Manchuria were virtually inconsequential, exposing Japan's claims of impending starvation as imperialist propaganda.

subfiles.about: Transmittal of a published study by Dr. Egerton Charles Grey on Japanese food supply, confirming the Embassy's view that Japan is self-sufficient and faces no food shortage.
subfiles.from: Charles MacVeagh, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Charles MacVeagh transmits a published article by Dr. Egerton Charles Grey reporting on his investigation into Japan's food problem for the League of Nations. MacVeagh highlights that the amount of rice consumed in sake brewing roughly equals annual rice imports, and that eliminating rice polishing would save an additional ten percent. He also observes that land converted to mulberry bushes during the silk boom could produce 50 million bushels of rice during an emergency, firmly supporting the conclusion that Japan suffers from no genuine food shortage.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 598 from Ambassador Charles MacVeagh on Food Conditions in Japan

subfiles.about: Statistical investigation by a League of Nations specialist showing that Japan produces sufficient food to feed its population and is virtually self-supporting.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Egerton Charles Grey summarizes his investigation for the Health Section of the League of Nations into whether the quantity of food in Japan is adequate for its population. Drawing on official statistical returns from 1915 to 1926, Grey shows that net imports of foodstuffs represent less than five percent of national consumption, an amount smaller than the normal wastage caused by rice polishing and cereal distillation into alcohol. He evaluates Japan's rich marine products, vegetable production, and harvest stability, concluding that there is no quantitative food shortage in Japan and that fears of starvation are groundless.
subfiles.title: Article by Dr. Egerton Charles Grey: 'The Food Problem In Japan: I.—Quantity: There Is No Food Shortage In Japan'

subfiles.about: Second page of a consular transmittal letter submitting an official economic report and a separate popular article on Japan's food import dependency.
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.summary: This concluding page of a consular despatch from American Consul E. R. Dickover in Kobe explains his submission of two enclosures: a comprehensive statistical report in quintuplicate and an article in duplicate drafted in a more lively format suitable for publication. Dickover notes the value of disseminating the facts on Japan's food situation to counter widespread misconceptions. The document includes consular file numbers and administrative routing instructions for copies to be forwarded to the U.S. Embassy and Consulate General in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Covering Despatch (Page 2) from Consul E. R. Dickover Transmitting Report and Article on Foodstuffs

subfiles.about: Consular economic report demonstrating that Japan's per capita food imports are among the lowest in the world and that dependence on Manchurian foodstuffs is negligible.
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul E. R. Dickover presents a detailed comparative statistical analysis demonstrating that Japan's dependence on imported foodstuffs is significantly lower than that of Western European nations and the United States. Utilizing trade statistics from 1929 and subsequent years, Dickover shows that Japan's net per capita food imports were only $0.91, compared to $49.99 for Great Britain, $12.07 for Germany, and $1.69 for the United States, with Japan's figures declining further through 1931 due to chemical fertilizer adoption and bumper harvests. Crucially, Dickover analyzes imports from Manchuria and Kwantung Leased Territory, revealing that when non-food industrial soya beans are excluded, net annual food imports from Manchuria amounted to just four cents per capita, demolishing claims that Manchuria constitutes an indispensable food 'life-line'.
subfiles.title: Report by Consul E. R. Dickover: 'Japan's Dependence Upon Imported Foodstuffs, In Comparison with Other Countries'

subfiles.about: Consular essay examining and debunking the myth that Japan faces imminent starvation and must expand into Manchuria to feed its population.
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.summary: In an article written in an accessible, engaging style, Consul E. R. Dickover critiques the psychological power of repeated propaganda that has convinced international observers that the 'wolf is at Japan's door.' He contrasts Japan's low import dependency with heavily import-dependent European nations like Great Britain, Switzerland, and Belgium, none of which use population density to justify territorial conquest. Highlighting rapid increases in crop yields spurred by chemical fertilizers and agricultural expansion in Hokkaido, Dickover concludes that Japan's net annual food imports from Manchuria amount to no more than a single small meal per person, exposing the 'life-line' rationale for Manchurian expansion as completely baseless.
subfiles.title: Article by Consul E. R. Dickover: 'The Wolf at Japan's Door'
